verses.text: Yahweh said to Joshua, “Don’t be afraid, and don’t be dismayed. Take all the warriors with you, and arise, go up to Ai. Behold, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, with his people, his city, and his land.
You shall do to Ai and her king as you did to Jericho and her king, except you shall take its goods and its livestock for yourselves. Set an ambush for the city behind it.”
So Joshua arose, with all the warriors, to go up to Ai. Joshua chose thirty thousand men, the mighty men of valor, and sent them out by night.
He commanded them, saying, “Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind the city. Don’t go very far from the city, but all of you be ready.
I and all the people who are with me will approach to the city. It shall happen, when they come out against us, as at the first, that we will flee before them.
They will come out after us, until we have drawn them away from the city; for they will say, ‘They flee before us, like the first time.’ So we will flee before them,
and you shall rise up from the ambush, and take possession of the city; for Yahweh your God will deliver it into your hand.
It shall be, when you have seized the city, that you shall set the city on fire. You shall do this according to Yahweh’s word. Behold, I have commanded you.”
Joshua sent them out; and they went to set up the ambush, and stayed between Bethel and Ai, on the west side of Ai; but Joshua stayed among the people that night.
Joshua rose up early in the morning, mustered the people, and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai.
All the people, even the men of war who were with him, went up, and came near, and came before the city, and encamped on the north side of Ai. Now there was a valley between him and Ai.
He took about five thousand men, and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, on the west side of the city.
So they set the people, even all the army who was on the north of the city, and their ambush on the west of the city; and Joshua went that night into the middle of the valley.

When the king of Ai saw it, they hurried and rose up early, and the men of the city went out against Israel to battle, he and all his people, at the time appointed, before the Arabah; but he didn’t know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.
Joshua and all Israel made as if they were beaten before them, and fled by the way of the wilderness.
All the people who were in the city were called together to pursue after them. They pursued Joshua, and were drawn away from the city.
There was not a man left in Ai or Beth El who didn’t go out after Israel. They left the city open, and pursued Israel.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand.” Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.
The ambush arose quickly out of their place, and they ran as soon as he had stretched out his hand, and entered into the city, and took it. They hurried and set the city on fire.

When the men of Ai looked behind them, they saw, and behold, the smoke of the city ascended up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that way. The people who fled to the wilderness turned back on the pursuers.
When Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had taken the city, and that the smoke of the city ascended, then they turned again, and killed the men of Ai.
The others came out of the city against them, so they were in the middle of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. They struck them, so that they let none of them remain or escape.
They captured the king of Ai alive, and brought him to Joshua.

When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the field, in the wilderness in which they pursued them, and they had all fallen by the edge of the sword, until they were consumed, all Israel returned to Ai, and struck it with the edge of the sword.
All that fell that day, both of men and women, were twelve thousand, even all the men of Ai.
For Joshua didn’t draw back his hand, with which he stretched out the javelin, until he had utterly destroyed all the inhabitants of Ai.
Israel took for themselves only the livestock and the goods of that city, according to Yahweh’s word which he commanded Joshua.
So Joshua burned Ai, and made it a heap forever, even a desolation, to this day.

He hanged the king of Ai on a tree until the evening, and at sundown Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree, and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city, and raised a great heap of stones on it that remains to this day.
Then Joshua built an altar to Yahweh, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal,

as Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded the children of Israel, as it is written in the book of the law of Moses, an altar of uncut stones, on which no one had lifted up any iron. They offered burnt offerings on it to Yahweh and sacrificed peace offerings.
He wrote there on the stones a copy of Moses’ law, which he wrote in the presence of the children of Israel.

All Israel, their elders and officers, and their judges, stood on both sides of the ark before the priests the Levites, who carried the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, the foreigner as well as the native; half of them in front of Mount Gerizim, and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of Yahweh had commanded at the first, that they should bless the people of Israel.
Afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the book of the law.
There was not a word of all that Moses commanded, which Joshua didn’t read before all the assembly of Israel, with the women, the little ones, and the foreigners who were among them.

footnotes.content: How tender that Yahweh speaks to Joshua after the sting of Ai's defeat. He doesn't scold him for Achan's hidden sin—He first heals his fear. Before strategy, the Lord gives courage. Our faith starts there, too: the God who restores us is the God who calls us forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jericho fell under the ban, but Ai is different. The Lord still judges sin, yet He graciously allows spoil this time. I see a picture of our Lord: in Christ, the ban of condemnation is fully borne, and by grace we share in the spoil of His victory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua doesn't sulk or send a smaller force in cowardice. He rises, chooses thirty thousand mighty men, and goes by night. Obedience after failure looks like this: a quiet rising, a wise plan, and trust that Yahweh still goes with him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ambush needs patience as much as courage. Joshua tells them to stay near but hidden, ready. So often the Lord's way of saving His people is not brute force alone, but faithful, hidden obedience. How like our Savior, who often works quietly to deliver us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua willingly makes himself bait. The leader walks out before the people to draw the enemy away. I can't help but think of our true Joshua, Jesus, who went out first for us, drawing our greatest enemies away from His people to meet them on the cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of Ai fall for the old trick because pride makes them sure of victory. Deception is used here to humble the proud. The Lord knows how to turn the confidence of the wicked back on itself, yet He never uses trickery against His own—He always keeps His promises to them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The secret is plain: the ambush will rise, but only because "Yahweh your God will deliver it into your hand." Victory belongs to Him. Our part is faithfulness; the power is His. That is the rest of God's people, then and now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They are told to seize the city and set it on fire according to Yahweh's word. Obedience here is complete—no picking and choosing. The same Lord who gives the command also gives the strength. When He says, "I have commanded you," His command is enough to carry us through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While the men go to ambush between Bethel and Ai, Joshua stays among the people that night. A good leader stays near his people in the tense hours before battle. Our great Leader, Jesus, has gone before us and yet draws near to us in every hour of waiting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua rises early, musters the people, and goes up with the elders before them. After failure at Ai, there is no sulking—just renewed trust and godly order. Godly leaders lead by example, and ours leads us all the way to the victory He has already won.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the warriors go up and encamp on the north side, with a valley between them and Ai. The setup is deliberate. The Lord often uses natural barriers and timing to show that the battle is His. When the odds look arranged by God, our faith learns to rest in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five thousand more are placed in ambush on the west side. The Lord is not stingy with help for His people. He orders every detail for their deliverance. So for those who belong to Jesus, no detail of our salvation or our preservation has been left to chance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua himself goes into the middle of the valley that night. The commander shares the risk with his men. How much more has our Commander, Jesus, shared our risk—becoming like us to rescue us, and going into the valley of death for His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Ai hurries out at the appointed time, confident and ignorant of the ambush. Overconfidence blinds us to God's hidden work. How grateful I am that our salvation did not depend on the enemy's ignorance, but on the wisdom of God in sending Jesus to save us while we were enemies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua and Israel feign defeat and flee by the way of the wilderness. It looks like the very thing that shamed them at Ai the first time. But now it's holy strategy. Sometimes the path of faith looks like retreat before it looks like victory—just as the cross looked like defeat before the resurrection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the men of Ai are drawn away in hot pursuit, leaving the city wide open. The bait works because of their eagerness to crush Israel again. The enemy rushes in where God has prepared the trap of mercy for His people and judgment for the proud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not a man is left in Ai or Bethel to guard the city—they all go out after Israel. In their zeal to destroy God's people, they leave themselves defenseless. How true it is that those who fight against the Lord fight against their own safety; those who rest in Christ are safe forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh tells Joshua to stretch out the javelin toward Ai, and the victory will be His. The signal is small, but obedience moves mountains when backed by God's word. Our signal of hope is far greater: Christ lifted up on the cross, and through Him all God's promises are yes and amen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At Joshua's outstretched hand, the ambush rushes in and sets the city on fire. The timing is perfect because it is God's timing. When the Lord gives the word, things move swiftly for the deliverance of His people. He is never late to save those who trust in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of Ai see the smoke rising to heaven and find their way of escape is cut off. There is no way to go back to the city, and no way to run from judgment. By contrast, those who flee to our true Joshua find that every way of escape from God's wrath has been opened for them in Jesus alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Joshua and Israel see the smoke, they turn back and strike Ai. What looked like flight becomes the turn of victory. God delights to reverse our shame. He who once allowed us to be turned back in defeat will, in Christ, turn us back to complete victory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ai is caught between Israel coming from the wilderness and the ambush coming from the city. There is no escape for those under God's judgment. I shudder at that, yet rejoice that all God's judgment for His people fell on Jesus, who was caught in the middle for us and took the full blow in our place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Ai is taken alive and brought to Joshua. Even the proudest among them is brought low before God's servant. One day every knee will bow before our greater Joshua, Jesus Christ, and every tongue confess that He alone is Lord to the glory of God the Father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel finishes the task in the field and wilderness, returns to Ai, and strikes it with the sword. The work of judgment is thorough, done at Yahweh's command. That solemn reality only makes the grace of the cross sweeter: for those in Jesus, our judgment is finished once for all in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve thousand fall that day, all the men of Ai. This is heavy to read. The Canaanite judgment is severe, yet it points us to a far greater and final judgment. Praise God that He has appointed a day when justice and mercy will meet fully at the cross for His people and fully in justice for all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua does not draw back his hand until the work of destruction is complete. His obedience is steady to the end. How blessed we are that our Joshua, Jesus, did not draw back His hand from the work of our salvation until He cried, "It is finished!" and our redemption was complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel takes only the livestock and goods as Yahweh commanded. They obey in the matter of spoil, unlike Achan before. Obedience grows from trust. When we believe the Lord will care for us, we are freed to obey Him, rather than grasping what He has told us to leave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ai becomes a heap forever, a desolation to this day. The city that exalted itself against the Lord is brought low. Every stronghold raised against God will come to ruin, but the house built on the Rock—those who trust in Jesus—will stand when all else falls away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Ai is hanged on a tree until evening, his body cast at the gate under a heap of stones. Deuteronomy speaks of a curse for one hung on a tree. Centuries later, our Savior bore that very curse for us, hung on a tree, so that the shame and judgment we deserved would be heaped on Him and removed from His people forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After victory, the very first thing Joshua does is build an altar to Yahweh on Mount Ebal. This is in obedience to Moses (Deuteronomy 27:4-8). I love it: worship comes first, not spoils. For those redeemed by Jesus, our first joy is always to worship the God who has given us the victory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones, as Moses commanded, offering burnt offerings and peace offerings to Yahweh. No tool is lifted to the stones, a reminder that the worship of God rests not on human workmanship, but on His own provision. How true in Jesus, our once-for-all offering and our true peace with God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua writes a copy of the law of Moses on the stones in the presence of Israel. The people stand before the Word that defines their life. God's people need to see His Word written before them. We are blessed to have the whole counsel of God in Scripture, pointing us to Jesus, the living Word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All Israel stands before the ark—elders, officers, judges, foreigners and natives alike—half before Gerizim for blessing, half before Ebal for curse. The congregation is whole and includes the foreigner who clings to Yahweh. In Jesus, our true ark of the covenant, strangers from every nation are brought near and share in His blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua reads all the words of the law—the blessing and the curse. Israel must hear both. Without the curse, we would never flee to the blessing; without seeing our guilt, we would never prize the One who bore the curse for us. Jesus took the curse so that we might receive the blessing of God forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of this moment: the whole assembly—men, women, little ones, and foreigners—gathers to hear every word of the Lord. As of 2026-10, I am grateful that through Jesus our greater Joshua, even the youngest and the stranger may hear the gospel and belong to God's people forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
